title: Why the Khalsa Cannot Be Subdued

blocks.text: The answer to Nadir's inquiry describes the Sikhs as a people who live lightly, move constantly, and refuse the comforts by which ordinary armies are tamed. They sleep with weapons near them, endure hunger without complaint, and treat hardship as part of their discipline rather than as a cause for surrender.

The page insists that persecution has trained the Khalsa into unusual cohesion: where one Sikh appears, many more seem ready to rise. Its argument climaxes in the claim that people sheltered by such a Lord cannot be defeated, because their courage is understood as a gift of divine protection rather than mere stubbornness.

That logic also turns history into proof. Those who opposed the Guru's light are remembered as fading away, while the Panth survives precisely because its confidence is tied to the Guru and not to possession of territory alone.
